## Setting up the physics

**Energy balance → salt mass.** For a two-tank sensible-heat system using standard "solar salt" (60% NaNO₃ / 40% KNO₃), with hot tank at 565°C and cold tank at 290°C (standard CSP operating window, ΔT = 275°C), c_p ≈ 1.5 kJ/kg·K, ρ ≈ 1900 kg/m³ (molten):

- E = 5,000 kWh = 1.8×10¹⁰ J
- m = E / (c_p·ΔT) = 1.8×10¹⁰ / (1,500 × 275) ≈ **43.6 tonnes** of salt
- Volume ≈ 23 m³ of salt → two tanks (hot + cold) sized ~28 m³ each with ullage

That's a *small* system — comparable in scale to a single large containerized Li-ion unit (a Tesla Megapack is ~3.9 MWh). This matters: TES economics are famously scale-favorable (tank shell cost scales with surface area, energy scales with volume), and the oft-quoted $20–30/kWh-thermal figures for molten-salt storage come from CSP plants at **500–1,500 MWh** — 100–300× bigger than this unit. At 5 MWh, fixed fabrication/engineering costs dominate and that discount disappears.

## Bottom-up BOM for the 5 MWh unit

| Item | Basis | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Solar salt | 43.6 t × $800/t | $35,000 |
| Hot tank (high-temp alloy, insulated, refractory-lined, shop-built) | small-batch custom vessel | $120,000 |
| Cold tank (carbon steel, insulated) | | $40,000 |
| Foundations | | $20,000 |
| Salt pumps ×2 (candle/sump, high-temp) | $20–30k each | $60,000 |
| Piping, valves, freeze-protection trace heating | molten salt needs active freeze protection | $80,000 |
| Charge/discharge heat exchangers | 2 units, ~1 MWth | $150,000 |
| Resistive immersion heaters (electric charging) | ~$50/kW | $50,000 |
| Controls/instrumentation | | $40,000 |
| Electrical (switchgear etc.) | | $30,000 |
| **Equipment subtotal** | | **$625,000** |
| Installation/erection (~30%) | | $180,000 |
| Engineering (~15%, high at small scale) | | $90,000 |
| Contingency (~10%) | | $60,000 |
| **Total — storage vessel only** | | **≈ $955,000** |

**→ ≈ $190/kWh of thermal storage capacity**, excluding any means of converting that heat back to electricity. That's already ~7–10× the literature figure for GWh-scale CSP tankage — the small-scale penalty is real and large.

## If the comparison is to Li-ion (electricity-in, electricity-out)

A thermal store alone isn't an electricity-storage system. To be comparable to a battery you need a **power block** to turn the heat back into electricity (a "Carnot battery"). At 1 MWe scale, a small steam/ORC turbine-generator runs ~$1,500–2,500/kW (small turbomachinery doesn't get utility-scale discounts either):

- Power block (1 MWe, $2,000/kW): **+$2,000,000**
- **Total installed ≈ $2.95M → ≈ $590/kWh** of electrical energy capacity

Round-trip efficiency is the other problem:
- Resistive heating: ~98%
- Thermal losses (small tank, higher surface/volume than utility scale): ~95% same-day
- Small heat-engine discharge (565°C hot side, real-world small turbine/ORC, not Carnot-ideal): ~30%
- **RTE ≈ 0.98 × 0.95 × 0.30 ≈ 28%**

versus Li-ion's ~90–95%.

## Levelized cost per kWh delivered

Assume 25-year life, 1 cycle/day → 9,125 cycles (thermal/mechanical cycling is not the limiting factor for molten salt — CSP plants routinely do this for decades).

**Molten salt (as electricity storage):**
- Electric energy delivered/cycle = 5,000 kWh × 0.28 = 1,400 kWh
- Lifetime delivered ≈ 1,400 × 9,125 ≈ 12.8M kWh
- Capital component = $2.95M / 12.8M kWh ≈ **$0.23/kWh**
- Plus input electricity cost ÷ RTE: at $0.08/kWh grid power → $0.08/0.28 ≈ $0.29/kWh
- Plus O&M (turbine overhauls etc.) ≈ $0.05–0.07/kWh
- **Total ≈ $0.55–0.60/kWh delivered**

**Li-ion (5 MWh, ~$180/kWh installed = $900k, RTE 90%, 5,000 cycles):**
- Lifetime delivered ≈ 5,000 × 0.90 × 5,000 ≈ 22.5M kWh
- Capital component = $900k / 22.5M kWh ≈ $0.04/kWh
- Input energy cost: $0.08/0.90 ≈ $0.089/kWh
- O&M ≈ $0.01/kWh
- **Total ≈ $0.14/kWh delivered**

## Verdict

At 5 MWh, molten-salt TES is **not** cost-competitive with lithium-ion for electricity storage — roughly 3–4× more expensive on a levelized $/kWh-delivered basis, and worse on raw installed $/kWh (~$590/kWh vs ~$180/kWh). Two compounding reasons: it never reaches the scale where tank economics pay off, and converting the stored heat back to electricity through a small, inefficient power block (~28% RTE) multiplies the effective cost of every kWh you put in.

The calculus flips in two situations, neither of which applies here: **(1) scale** — at 100s of MWh–GWh (utility CSP, or Carnot-battery projects sized for industrial off-take), tank $/kWh falls toward the $20–30/kWh range and a full-size efficient steam turbine becomes affordable per kW; **(2) end use** — if the output is consumed directly as *heat* (process heat, district heating) rather than reconverted to electricity, you skip the power block entirely and the RTE penalty disappears, which is exactly why real-world "thermal battery" plays (e.g., Rondo Energy) target industrial heat customers instead of competing head-on with Li-ion on the grid.
